content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed comprehensive guidelines to support the prevention and control of HIV infections and the management of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) within the health sector. These guidelines aim to consolidate, prioritize, and describe key indicators for monitoring both national and global health sector responses to HIV. The primary goal is to assist countries in selecting, collecting, and systematically analyzing strategic information to guide their health sector strategies in addressing HIV. The publication emphasizes that the designations and presentation of material do not reflect any opinion by WHO regarding the legal status of countries, territories, cities, or their authorities, nor do they address the delimitation of borders. Any mention of specific companies or products does not imply endorsement or preference by WHO over others of a similar nature. While every effort has been made to verify the accuracy of the information, the material is distributed without any warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. WHO is not liable for any damages arising from the use of this material. The guidelines include detailed tables, figures, and frameworks to support the health sector's response to HIV. These include the result chain for health sector responses, the cascade of HIV prevention, care, and treatment services, and global indicators for monitoring and evaluating health sector outcomes. Specific focus areas include disaggregated HIV data, the ART (antiretroviral therapy) cascade, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and the integration of care for HIV and tuberculosis co-infections. The guidelines also address the importance of strategic information capacity, accountability, and achieving the 90–90–90 targets (90% of people living with HIV knowing their status, 90% of those diagnosed receiving sustained ART, and 90% of those on ART achieving viral suppression). The development of these guidelines involved extensive collaboration with global experts, technical working groups, and contributors from various organizations, including UNAIDS, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and numerous ministries of health worldwide. The guidelines were supported by funding from the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH, among others. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of its staff, consultants, and external experts who provided technical writing, editing, and administrative support. The guidelines aim to provide a unified and prioritized approach to monitoring and evaluating HIV responses, ensuring that all indicators are consolidated in one place and linked to a result chain to guide decision-making and improve health outcomes globally.
